One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index

Yegor Baranovski ††thanks: Email: yegorbar01@gmail.com. I thank Scott Nelson for posing the question that motivated this paper.
November 10, 2026
Abstract

AUC and the Brier score are standard summaries of a binary risk score, yet they can rank models differently. We introduce a weighted AUC, AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, which weights each pair of observations by how differently a decision maker with probability of acting π\pi treats them. We show that all three are built on weighted averages of one curve, the Youden index J⁡(t)=TPR⁡(t)−FPR⁡(t)J(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)-\mathrm{FPR}(t) across cutoffs tt, and that the averages differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. Each weights a cutoff by how much something rises across it: for AUC, the distribution of all scores; for the Brier score, the true probability 𝔼⁡[Y∣S]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid S]; for AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, the decision maker’s probability of acting. Up to normalization, AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved to the cutoffs the decision maker cares about. We also show that weighting pairs by |π⁡(s)−π⁡(s′)||\pi(s)-\pi(s^{\prime})| is, up to scale, the only pair weight fixed in advance that makes a pair-weighted AUC an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution. As a ranking measure, AUC weights every model the same way. Hand (2009) shows that it can also be read as an average over cost thresholds, and in that reading each model weights the thresholds differently. The numerator of AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, which we call the policy Youden index, is the expected share of class 1 a fixed policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It judges every model by the same policy and so avoids this; the full ratio AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} does not.

1 Introduction

Models judged by AUC or the Brier score can be used to decide who to act on. A lender’s default model decides who to approve, a hospital’s risk model who to treat, a bank’s fraud model which payments to block, and a weather service’s rain forecast when to issue a warning. So the natural question is what each measure rewards, in terms of the decisions the score supports.

This paper answers that question with one object, which we call the Youden curve. A cutoff tt acts on every observation with a score above tt. Its Youden index J⁡(t)=TPR⁡(t)−FPR⁡(t)J(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)-\mathrm{FPR}(t) is the share of class 1 it acts on minus the share of class 0 (Youden, 1950). Each cutoff is a decision, and J⁡(t)J(t) measures its performance. JJ does not depend on the base rate. A measure that does not commit to one cutoff must average JJ across cutoffs, and describe how much each cutoff counts. We show that three measures are built on exactly such averages, and that they differ in the weights they put on the cutoffs. For a nondecreasing weight ww with values in [0,1][0,1], let TwT_{w} be a random cutoff with CDF ww, so 𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tw)]\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})] is the average of JJ with each cutoff weighted by how much ww rises across it. Write SyS_{y} for the score of a class-yy observation, r⁡(s)=P⁡(Y=1∣S=s)r(s)=P(Y=1\mid S=s) for the true probability, pp for a forecast of it, π⁡(s)\pi(s) for the decision maker’s probability of acting on score ss, and FmidF^{\mathrm{mid}} for the CDF of the scores with ties split in half.

  1. 1.

    AUC weights each cutoff by how much the distribution of all scores rises across it. This is the same as counting every share of observations acted on equally (Theorem 1):

    AUC=12+𝔼⁡[J⁡(TFmid)].\mathrm{AUC}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\mathbb{E}[J(T_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}})].
  2. 2.

    The Brier score weights each cutoff by how much the true probability rr rises across it. This is the same as counting every risk threshold equally, since the thresholds that lead to a cutoff span exactly that rise. It adds a penalty for a forecast that is not ideal (Theorem 2):

    BS=𝔼⁡[(p−r)2]+Var⁡(Y)​(1−𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tr)]).\mathrm{BS}=\mathbb{E}[(p-r)^{2}]+\mathrm{Var}(Y)\bigl(1-\mathbb{E}[J(T_{r})]\bigr).

    For the ideal forecast p=rp=r, the Brier skill score is 𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tr)]\mathbb{E}[J(T_{r})] (Corollary 1).

  3. 3.

    AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} weights each pair of a class-0 and a class-1 observation, with scores ss and s′s^{\prime}, by |π⁡(s)−π⁡(s′)||\pi(s)-\pi(s^{\prime})|, how differently the decision maker treats them. It weights each cutoff by how much π\pi rises across it (Theorem 3):

    AUCπ=12+𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tπ)]2​𝔼​|π⁡(S1)−π⁡(S0)|.\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[J(T_{\pi})]}{2\,\mathbb{E}|\pi(S_{1})-\pi(S_{0})|}.

All three follow from one identity, 𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tw)]=𝔼⁡[w⁡(S1)]−𝔼⁡[w⁡(S0)]\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]=\mathbb{E}[w(S_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[w(S_{0})] (Lemma 3). All results hold for discrete scores with ties.

Theorem 4 explains this choice of pair weight. If a pair-weighted AUC with weights fixed in advance is an average of the Youden curve for every score distribution, its pair weight must be a multiple of |w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)||w(s)-w(s^{\prime})| for some ww, which then dictates its cutoff weight. So choosing pair weights is choosing cutoff weights. Plain AUC gives every pair equal weight, and its cutoff weights come from the model’s own scores, so, in terms of risk thresholds, they change when the model changes.

Since each measure averages JJ over cutoffs, choosing a measure means choosing how much each decision matters. AUC weights equally acting on the top 10%, the top 20%, and so on. The Brier score weights equally acting on everyone whose true probability is above 10%, above 20%, and so on. It also charges for a forecast that is not ideal, even when the decisions depend only on the ranking. AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} gives each decision the weight the decision maker gives it, and like AUC it does not need the score to be a probability. Up to normalization, AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast with its weight moved from where rr rises to where π\pi rises; when π\pi is linear in rr, it is exactly a rescaled Brier skill score (Proposition 1). The normalization does depend on the model, so to compare models we use the numerator, which we call the policy Youden index, Jπ=𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tπ)]J_{\pi}=\mathbb{E}[J(T_{\pi})]: the expected share of class 1 the policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0 (Section 5).

Section 2 sets up the Youden curve. Section 3 states the cutoff lemma and the three results. Section 4 characterizes the pair weights. Section 5 takes up Hand’s coherence critique with a worked example, shows why models should be compared by the policy Youden index, and extends the point to comparisons across groups. Section 6 concludes, and the proofs are in Appendix A.

1.1 Related work

Measures as averages over cutoffs.

The closest work is Hernández-Orallo et al. (2012), who write AUC, the Brier score and other measures as expected classification loss under different rules for choosing the cutoff (Flach et al., 2011, for AUC, see also). Hand (2009) shows that AUC is a linear function of the average minimum loss over a cost distribution that depends on the classifier itself, and proposes the H-measure with a fixed cost distribution instead. Schervish (1989) shows that every proper scoring rule, the Brier score among them, is a mixture of cost-weighted losses over cutoffs on the probability scale. We average a different quantity, JJ, which does not depend on the base rate or on costs, so every measure becomes an average of the same curve. Theorem 1 then gives Hand’s diagnosis in Youden terms: AUC’s weight is the model’s own score distribution, which puts equal weight on every share acted on, and Theorem 2 keeps Schervish’s uniform thresholds but applies them to the true probability rr rather than the forecast.

Earlier averages of JJ.

Averages of JJ have appeared for two weights. The first is uniform over risk thresholds, the Brier weight of Corollary 1: Pencina et al. (2008) describe the integrated discrimination improvement, a difference of two discrimination slopes, as an integrated difference in Youden indices. The second is the pooled score distribution, where AUC is 12\tfrac{1}{2} plus the area under the KS curve (Adeodato and Melo, 2022). What is new here is the single identity for an arbitrary weight, which recovers both as special cases. We also introduce AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} as a measure of discrimination at the decision maker’s own cutoffs, and characterize its pair weights. Its numerator, the policy Youden index JπJ_{\pi}, judges every model by the same policy, so it avoids Hand’s objection without a cost model or a probability forecast, while the ratio AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} does not.

Decision-weighted measures.

Other measures weight a payoff by a distribution of decision thresholds. One such payoff is the net benefit of Vickers and Elkin (2006). Talluri and Shete (2016) weight net benefit by a distribution of thresholds estimated from observed clinical decisions, and Zhu et al. (2025) weight the Brier score by a distribution of thresholds. These measures also depend on calibration, not only on the ranking. Weighted AUCs already exist. Li and Fine (2010) weight the ROC curve by a density on specificity, and Wieand et al. (1989) average sensitivity over a distribution on that same axis. Those weights sit on the false-positive axis. AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} weights each pair by how differently the policy treats its two scores, which puts the weight on the score scale, so the score need not be a probability and only discrimination is measured. Theorem 4 says this is the only pair weight, fixed in advance, that makes the result an average of JJ.

2 Setup

Each observation has a score SS and a binary label Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\}, with ρ=P⁡(Y=1)∈(0,1)\rho=P(Y=1)\in(0,1). The score is the output of the model being evaluated, with higher scores meaning class 1 is more likely. It need not be a probability. Comparing models means comparing different scores SS for the same observations. A decision maker either takes an action or does not; the action is aimed at class 1. Write Fy​(t)=P⁡(S≤t∣Y=y)F_{y}(t)=P(S\leq t\mid Y=y) for the CDF of class yy, and F⁡(t)=P⁡(S≤t)=(1−ρ)​F0​(t)+ρ​F1​(t)F(t)=P(S\leq t)=(1-\rho)F_{0}(t)+\rho F_{1}(t) for the CDF of all scores. The score may have any distribution; in particular it may be discrete, so ties are allowed. Write Fmid​(t)=P⁡(S<t)+12​P​(S=t)F^{\mathrm{mid}}(t)=P(S<t)+\tfrac{1}{2}P(S=t) for the mid-point version of FF, the share of scores strictly below tt plus half the share tied at tt, and define FymidF^{\mathrm{mid}}_{y} the same way within class yy. For continuous scores Fmid=FF^{\mathrm{mid}}=F. Let S0∼F0S_{0}\sim F_{0} and S1∼F1S_{1}\sim F_{1} be independent: the scores of a random class-0 and a random class-1 observation.

Assumption 1 (Monotonicity).

r⁡(s)=P⁡(Y=1∣S=s)r(s)=P(Y=1\mid S=s) is nondecreasing in ss.

Monotonicity is a condition on the two classes together, not on F0F_{0} or F1F_{1} alone. With class densities f0f_{0} and f1f_{1} it is equivalent, by Bayes’ rule, to the likelihood ratio f1/f0f_{1}/f_{0} being nondecreasing: the higher the score, the more it looks like class 1. It is what makes acting on high scores sensible.

2.1 The ROC curve and the Youden curve

A score is used through cutoffs: the decision maker acts on every observation whose score is high enough. The cutoff “act when S>tS>t” acts on a share of each class, the true positive rate and the false positive rate:

TPR⁡(t)=P⁡(S>t∣Y=1)=1−F1​(t),FPR⁡(t)=P⁡(S>t∣Y=0)=1−F0​(t).\mathrm{TPR}(t)=P(S>t\mid Y=1)=1-F_{1}(t),\qquad\mathrm{FPR}(t)=P(S>t\mid Y=0)=1-F_{0}(t).

As tt moves from +∞+\infty to −∞-\infty, the point (FPR⁡(t),TPR⁡(t))(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)) traces the ROC curve from (0,0)(0,0) to (1,1)(1,1) (Figure 1). The Youden index of the cutoff is the share of class 1 it acts on minus the share of class 0,

J⁡(t)=TPR⁡(t)−FPR⁡(t)=(1−F1​(t))−(1−F0​(t))=F0​(t)−F1​(t),J(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)-\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\bigl(1-F_{1}(t)\bigr)-\bigl(1-F_{0}(t)\bigr)=F_{0}(t)-F_{1}(t),

the vertical gap between the ROC curve and the diagonal. The diagonal is the line TPR=FPR\mathrm{TPR}=\mathrm{FPR}, so directly below the point (FPR⁡(t),TPR⁡(t))(\mathrm{FPR}(t),\mathrm{TPR}(t)) it is at height FPR⁡(t)\mathrm{FPR}(t). As a function of tt, we call JJ the Youden curve (Figure 2). It is zero at both extremes, J⁡(±∞)=0J(\pm\infty)=0, since acting on everyone or on no one does not separate the classes. J⁡(t)J(t) is the gap between the two class CDFs at cutoff tt. Since J≥0J\geq 0 under Assumption 1 (Lemma 1), the largest J⁡(t)J(t) is the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) statistic (Kolmogorov, 1933; Smirnov, 1939).

Lemma 1 (JJ is nonnegative).

Under Assumption 1, F1​(t)≤F⁡(t)≤F0​(t)F_{1}(t)\leq F(t)\leq F_{0}(t) for every tt. Hence J⁡(t)≥0J(t)\geq 0 at every cutoff.

The proof is in Appendix A. A higher score never makes class 1 less likely, so the scores at or below any cutoff hold a smaller share of class 1 than of class 0, and the ROC curve never falls below the diagonal. Three facts make JJ the natural measure of how well one cutoff separates the classes.

  • •

    It is measured against random acting. Acting on each observation with the same probability, ignoring the score, reaches the same share of each class, so J=0J=0. So JJ is the extra share of class 1 a cutoff reaches compared with random acting that reaches the same share of class 0.

  • •

    It uses only shares within each class, so it does not depend on the base rate ρ\rho.

  • •

    It counts pairs. Pair a random class-0 observation with a random class-1 observation, so that P⁡(S0≤t)=F0​(t)P(S_{0}\leq t)=F_{0}(t) and P⁡(S1≤t)=F1​(t)P(S_{1}\leq t)=F_{1}(t). Splitting each by where the other member falls,

    F0​(t)=P⁡(S0≤t,S1≤t)+P⁡(S0≤t<S1),F1​(t)=P⁡(S0≤t,S1≤t)+P⁡(S1≤t<S0).F_{0}(t)=P(S_{0}\leq t,\,S_{1}\leq t)+P(S_{0}\leq t<S_{1}),\qquad F_{1}(t)=P(S_{0}\leq t,\,S_{1}\leq t)+P(S_{1}\leq t<S_{0}).

    Subtracting, the first terms cancel:

    J⁡(t)=P⁡(S0≤t<S1)−P⁡(S1≤t<S0),J(t)=P(S_{0}\leq t<S_{1})-P(S_{1}\leq t<S_{0}),

    the share of pairs that the cutoff splits correctly (class 1 acted on, class 0 not) minus the share it splits incorrectly. AUC also counts pairs, which is why the two are linked.

3.1 Averaging JJ over a weight’s cutoffs

Definition 1 (Weight).

A weight is a nondecreasing, right-continuous function w:ℝ→[0,1]w:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]. We interpret w⁡(s)w(s) as the probability of acting on an observation with score ss.

A weight decides how much each cutoff counts in the average. Nondecreasing means higher scores are acted on at least as often. A smooth ww is already right-continuous.

Lemma 2 (Weights on cutoffs).
  1. (a)

    Smooth case. If ww has a density w′w^{\prime}, then

    𝔼⁡[w⁡(S1)]−𝔼⁡[w⁡(S0)]=∫J⁡(t)​w′​(t)​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}[w(S_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[w(S_{0})]=\int J(t)\,w^{\prime}(t)\,dt.
  2. (b)

    Discrete case. If the scores take finitely many values s1<⋯<sns_{1}<\dots<s_{n}, then

    𝔼⁡[w⁡(S1)]−𝔼⁡[w⁡(S0)]=∑k=2n[w⁡(sk)−w⁡(sk−1)]​J​(sk−1).\mathbb{E}[w(S_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[w(S_{0})]=\sum_{k=2}^{n}\bigl[w(s_{k})-w(s_{k-1})\bigr]\,J(s_{k-1}).

The proof is in Appendix A. The left side is how much more often ww acts on class 1 than on class 0. The right side is the Youden curve weighted by w′w^{\prime}: cutoff tt counts in proportion to how fast ww rises there, and cutoffs where ww is flat don’t count at all. The discrete case is the same with w′​(t)​d​tw^{\prime}(t)\,dt replaced by the rise w⁡(sk)−w⁡(sk−1)w(s_{k})-w(s_{k-1}), and the integral replaced by a sum.

Definition 2 (Random cutoff).

Define a random variable TwT_{w} with values in [−∞,∞][-\infty,\infty], interpreted as a random cutoff, independent of (S0,S1)(S_{0},S_{1}), with CDF

FTw​(t)=P⁡(Tw≤t)={w⁡(−∞)t=−∞,w⁡(t)t∈ℝ,1t=+∞,F_{T_{w}}(t)=P(T_{w}\leq t)=\begin{cases}w(-\infty)&t=-\infty,\\ w(t)&t\in\mathbb{R},\\ 1&t=+\infty,\end{cases}

where w⁡(±∞)w(\pm\infty) are the limits of ww. The cutoff −∞-\infty acts on everyone and +∞+\infty on no one, so J⁡(±∞)=0J(\pm\infty)=0.

TwT_{w} is a cutoff drawn at random with CDF ww, and the rule acts when S>TwS>T_{w}. With discrete scores s1<⋯<sns_{1}<\dots<s_{n}, call a weight between-score if it has no jump at any sks_{k}. If ww jumps at a score, TwT_{w} can land on that score, and the rule then does not act there (Figure 3a). We deal with this by moving each jump to the midpoint between neighbouring scores, which keeps the values at the scores and removes the problem (Figure 3b). We only care about ww at the actual scores, so this is harmless. With discrete scores we always use this between-score version. The problem comes from the strict rule. Under “act when S≥TwS\geq T_{w}” it does not arise, but then TPR⁡(t)=1−P⁡(S1<t)\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-P(S_{1}<t) and JJ is no longer F0−F1F_{0}-F_{1}. We keep “act when S>tS>t” so that both keep their standard form.

For a between-score or continuous weight, P⁡(Tw<s)=w⁡(s)P(T_{w}<s)=w(s) at every score ss, so acting when s>Tws>T_{w} is the same as acting on score ss with probability w⁡(s)w(s). Random cutoffs are standard: the threshold choice methods of Hernández-Orallo et al. (2012) include cutoffs drawn uniformly over the range of scores and over predicted positive rates. What we add is the general weight ww and the identity below.

Lemma 3 (Cutoff lemma).

In either case of Lemma 2, with ww between-score in the discrete case, 𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tw)]=𝔼⁡[w⁡(S1)]−𝔼⁡[w⁡(S0)]\;\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]=\mathbb{E}[w(S_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[w(S_{0})].

The proof is in Appendix A. The left side is the weighted average of JJ over the cutoffs of ww, and the right side is how much more often ww acts on class 1 than on class 0. By Lemma 2, both equal

𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tw)]={∫J⁡(t)​w′​(t)​𝑑tif w is smooth,∑k=2n[w⁡(sk)−w⁡(sk−1)]​J​(sk−1)if the scores are discrete.\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int J(t)\,w^{\prime}(t)\,dt&\text{if $w$ is smooth},\\[10.0pt] \displaystyle\sum_{k=2}^{n}\bigl[w(s_{k})-w(s_{k-1})\bigr]\,J(s_{k-1})&\text{if the scores are discrete}.\end{cases}

For one weight the lemma is known. When ww is a predicted risk, 𝔼⁡[w⁡(S1)]−𝔼⁡[w⁡(S0)]\mathbb{E}[w(S_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[w(S_{0})] is the average predicted risk in class 1 minus that in class 0, called the discrimination slope. Pencina et al. (2008) show that the slope is the integral of JJ over risk thresholds in (0,1)(0,1), so the difference between two models’ slopes is an integrated difference of their Youden indices. Lemma 3 states it for every weight, and every result below is one choice of ww.

The results below hold in both cases of Lemma 2. With discrete scores, FmidF^{\mathrm{mid}}, rr and π\pi enter only through their values at the scores, and we use their between-score versions.

3.2 AUC

Definition 3 (AUC).

AUC=P⁡(S0<S1)+12​P​(S0=S1)\mathrm{AUC}=P(S_{0}<S_{1})+\tfrac{1}{2}P(S_{0}=S_{1}): the probability that a random class-1 observation outscores a random class-0 observation, with ties counted as half. This equals the area under the ROC curve, with its points joined by straight lines if the scores are discrete (Bamber, 1975; Hanley and McNeil, 1982).

Take the weight w=Fmidw=F^{\mathrm{mid}}. With scores that have a density ff, TFmidT_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}} is a cutoff distributed like the mix of scores, so a cutoff region counts in proportion to how many observations sit there:

𝔼⁡[J⁡(TFmid)]=∫J⁡(t)​f​(t)​𝑑t.\mathbb{E}[J(T_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}})]=\int J(t)\,f(t)\,dt.
Theorem 1 (AUC).

AUC=12+𝔼⁡[J⁡(TFmid)]\mathrm{AUC}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\mathbb{E}[J(T_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}})].

The proof is in Appendix A. AUC is the average Youden index with each cutoff weighted by how much the distribution of all scores rises across it. The mix of the two classes does not matter, as the same holds for w=(1−λ)​F0mid+λ​F1midw=(1-\lambda)F^{\mathrm{mid}}_{0}+\lambda F^{\mathrm{mid}}_{1} with any λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1], and FmidF^{\mathrm{mid}} is λ=ρ\lambda=\rho. For continuous scores F⁡(TF)F(T_{F}) is uniform on (0,1)(0,1), so the share of observations acted on, 1−F⁡(TF)1-F(T_{F}), is uniform too. Therefore, Theorem 1 says that AUC−12\mathrm{AUC}-\tfrac{1}{2} is the average JJ over decision makers who act on a uniformly random share of the population. The continuous case is known, stated as expected loss (Flach et al., 2011; Hernández-Orallo et al., 2012). The closest is that AUC is 12\tfrac{1}{2} plus the area under the KS curve (Adeodato and Melo, 2022). That curve is the Youden curve plotted against the pooled share F⁡(t)F(t) instead of tt. Equal widths on that axis are equal shares of observations, so its area is the average of JJ that Theorem 1 gives.

3.3 The Brier score

Definition 4 (Brier score).

Let p=p⁡(S)∈[0,1]p=p(S)\in[0,1] be a forecast of P⁡(Y=1∣S)P(Y=1\mid S). The Brier score is BS=𝔼⁡[(p−Y)2]\mathrm{BS}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(p-Y)^{2}\bigr], and the forecast is ideal if p=r=𝔼⁡[Y∣S]p=r=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid S]. The Brier skill score is BSS=1−BS/Var⁡(Y)\mathrm{BSS}=1-\mathrm{BS}/\mathrm{Var}(Y).

The ideal forecast minimizes BS\mathrm{BS} among all forecasts based on SS. By the decomposition of Murphy (1973), grouping observations by their score SS rather than by their forecast pp,

BS=𝔼⁡[(p−r)2]−Var⁡(r)+Var⁡(Y).\mathrm{BS}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(p-r)^{2}\bigr]-\mathrm{Var}(r)+\mathrm{Var}(Y).

For the ideal forecast, BS=Var⁡(Y)−Var⁡(r)\mathrm{BS}=\mathrm{Var}(Y)-\mathrm{Var}(r) and BSS=Var⁡(r)/Var⁡(Y)\mathrm{BSS}=\mathrm{Var}(r)/\mathrm{Var}(Y). Under Assumption 1, rr is itself a weight.

Theorem 2 (Brier score).

Under Assumption 1,

BS=𝔼⁡[(p−r)2]+Var⁡(Y)​(1−𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tr)]).\mathrm{BS}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(p-r)^{2}\bigr]+\mathrm{Var}(Y)\bigl(1-\mathbb{E}[J(T_{r})]\bigr).
Corollary 1.

For the ideal forecast, BSS=𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tr)]\mathrm{BSS}=\mathbb{E}[J(T_{r})].

The proofs are in Appendix A. The Brier score weights each cutoff by how much the true probability rr rises across it, and adds a separate term 𝔼⁡[(p−r)2]\mathbb{E}[(p-r)^{2}] for how far the forecast is from ideal.

On the score scale, the axis of cutoffs tt, the weights come from rr. On the probability scale, the axis of risk thresholds u=r⁡(t)u=r(t), they are equal. To see this, picture decision makers who each act on everyone whose true probability is above their own risk threshold uu. Many thresholds lead to the same decision. Take three scores with r⁡(s1)=0.1r(s_{1})=0.1, r⁡(s2)=0.3r(s_{2})=0.3 and r⁡(s3)=0.9r(s_{3})=0.9. Every uu between 0.1 and 0.3 acts on the top two scores, which is cutoff s1s_{1}. Every uu between 0.3 and 0.9 acts on the top score only, which is cutoff s2s_{2}. A uu below 0.1 acts on everyone and a uu above 0.9 on no one, and both give J=0J=0. If every threshold uu in [0,1][0,1] counts equally, cutoff s1s_{1} gets weight 0.3−0.1=0.20.3-0.1=0.2 and cutoff s2s_{2} gets 0.9−0.3=0.60.9-0.3=0.6. These are the rises in rr, the weights of Corollary 1. So the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast is the average Youden index over risk thresholds spread evenly on [0,1][0,1]. A threshold of 90% counts as much as one of 5%, even for a decision maker who only uses one of them. AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} instead puts the weight where the decision maker acts.

The Brier skill score of the ideal forecast, Var⁡(r)/Var⁡(Y)\mathrm{Var}(r)/\mathrm{Var}(Y), equals the gap in average true probability between the two classes, 𝔼⁡[r∣Y=1]−𝔼⁡[r∣Y=0]\mathbb{E}[r\mid Y=1]-\mathbb{E}[r\mid Y=0]. The proof of Theorem 2 in Appendix A shows this directly. Corollary 1 puts it on the score scale, and the comparison needs this form. There it is an average of the same Youden curve J⁡(t)J(t) as AUC and AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, so the three measures can be compared cutoff by cutoff and differ only in their weights.

This is close to the decision reading of Schervish (1989), which also averages over uniform thresholds. Schervish thresholds the forecast pp and averages a cost-weighted loss; Theorem 2 thresholds the true probability rr, averages the unweighted JJ, and puts the forecast’s error in the separate term 𝔼⁡[(p−r)2]\mathbb{E}[(p-r)^{2}].

3.4 AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w}

Definition 5 (AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w}).

AUC is the share of correctly ordered pairs, with every pair weighted equally:

AUC=𝔼[𝟏{S0<S1}+12𝟏{S0=S1}].\mathrm{AUC}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}<S_{1}\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}=S_{1}\}\bigr].

For a weight ww, let Δw=w⁡(S1)−w⁡(S0)\Delta_{w}=w(S_{1})-w(S_{0}), how differently ww treats the two members of a pair. Weighting each pair by |Δw||\Delta_{w}| instead of 11, and dividing by the total weight so the result is still a share, gives, assuming 𝔼​|Δw|>0\mathbb{E}|\Delta_{w}|>0,

AUCw=𝔼[|Δw| 1{S0<S1}]𝔼​|Δw|.\mathrm{AUC}_{w}=\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[|\Delta_{w}|\,\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}<S_{1}\}\bigr]}{\mathbb{E}|\Delta_{w}|}.

Tied pairs have Δw=0\Delta_{w}=0, so they need no tie term.

The measure of interest is AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, where π⁡(s)\pi(s) is the probability that the decision maker acts on an observation with score ss. We take π\pi to be nondecreasing, so it is a weight. A pair the decision maker treats the same way, both acted on or both not, cannot be misranked in any way that matters to that decision maker, and gets no weight.

Theorem 3 (AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w}).

For any weight ww with 𝔼​|Δw|>0\mathbb{E}|\Delta_{w}|>0,

AUCw=12+𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tw)]2​𝔼​|Δw|.\mathrm{AUC}_{w}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]}{2\,\mathbb{E}|\Delta_{w}|}.

The proof is in Appendix A. AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} therefore weights each cutoff by how much the decision maker’s probability of acting rises across it. Under Assumption 1, J≥0J\geq 0 at every cutoff (Lemma 1), so AUC and AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w} are at least 12\tfrac{1}{2} and the BSS\mathrm{BSS} of the ideal forecast is at least 00.

For the decision maker’s policy we call the numerator the policy Youden index,

Jπ=𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tπ)]=𝔼⁡[π⁡(S1)]−𝔼⁡[π⁡(S0)],J_{\pi}=\mathbb{E}[J(T_{\pi})]=\mathbb{E}[\pi(S_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[\pi(S_{0})],

the expected share of class 1 the policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. For a policy that acts above one cutoff tt, it is J⁡(t)J(t). JπJ_{\pi} is the Youden index of the randomized policy that acts on score ss with probability π⁡(s)\pi(s). It needs no costs and no forecast probability; a decision maker with a known cost ratio kk can use 𝔼⁡[TPR⁡(Tπ)−k​FPR​(Tπ)]=𝔼⁡[π⁡(S1)]−k​𝔼​[π⁡(S0)]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{TPR}(T_{\pi})-k\,\mathrm{FPR}(T_{\pi})]=\mathbb{E}[\pi(S_{1})]-k\,\mathbb{E}[\pi(S_{0})] instead. Section 5 shows that models should be compared by JπJ_{\pi} rather than by AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}.

3.5 Link to the Brier score

Proposition 1 (Link).

AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w} is unchanged if ww is replaced by α+β​w\alpha+\beta w with β>0\beta>0. Hence, under Assumption 1, if π=α+β​r\pi=\alpha+\beta r with β>0\beta>0,

AUCπ=AUCr=12+𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tr)]2​𝔼​|r⁡(S1)−r⁡(S0)|,\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}=\mathrm{AUC}_{r}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[J(T_{r})]}{2\,\mathbb{E}|r(S_{1})-r(S_{0})|},

and the numerator is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast.

The proof is in Appendix A. So when the decision maker’s probability of acting is linear in the true probability, AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} is the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast, rescaled. When it is not, AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} moves the weight to the cutoffs where decisions change.

4 Why weight pairs by |w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)||w(s)-w(s^{\prime})|

One could weight pairs by some other function of ww. To compare choices, define a general pair-weighted AUC.

Definition 6 (Pair-weighted AUC).

A pair weight is a bounded symmetric function W⁡(s,s′)≥0W(s,s^{\prime})\geq 0. Assuming 𝔼⁡[W⁡(S0,S1)]>0\mathbb{E}[W(S_{0},S_{1})]>0,

AUCW=𝔼[W(S0,S1)(𝟏{S0<S1}+12𝟏{S0=S1})]𝔼⁡[W⁡(S0,S1)].\mathrm{AUC}_{W}=\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[W(S_{0},S_{1})\bigl(\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}<S_{1}\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}=S_{1}\}\bigr)\bigr]}{\mathbb{E}[W(S_{0},S_{1})]}.

W≡1W\equiv 1 gives AUC, and W⁡(s,s′)=|w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)|W(s,s^{\prime})=|w(s)-w(s^{\prime})| gives AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w}.

Lemma 4 (Pair form).

For any pair weight WW,

AUCW=12+𝔼[W(S0,S1)(𝟏{S0<S1}−𝟏{S1<S0})]2​𝔼​[W⁡(S0,S1)].\mathrm{AUC}_{W}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\mathbb{E}\bigl[W(S_{0},S_{1})\bigl(\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}<S_{1}\}-\mathbf{1}\{S_{1}<S_{0}\}\bigr)\bigr]}{2\,\mathbb{E}[W(S_{0},S_{1})]}.

The proof is in Appendix A. The numerator is the weight of correctly ranked pairs minus the weight of incorrectly ranked pairs.

Averages of JJ are pair-weighted in exactly this form. Recall from Section 2 that JJ counts pairs, J⁡(t)=P⁡(S0≤t<S1)−P⁡(S1≤t<S0)J(t)=P(S_{0}\leq t<S_{1})-P(S_{1}\leq t<S_{0}). Replacing tt by TwT_{w}, which is independent of the pair,

𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tw)]=P⁡(S0≤Tw<S1)−P⁡(S1≤Tw<S0).\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]=P(S_{0}\leq T_{w}<S_{1})-P(S_{1}\leq T_{w}<S_{0}).

Fix a pair with class-0 score ss and class-1 score s′s^{\prime}. If s<s′s<s^{\prime}, TwT_{w} splits it correctly when it lands in [s,s′)[s,s^{\prime}), which has probability P⁡(s≤Tw<s′)=w⁡(s′)−w⁡(s)P(s\leq T_{w}<s^{\prime})=w(s^{\prime})-w(s). If s>s′s>s^{\prime}, it splits it incorrectly with probability w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)w(s)-w(s^{\prime}), and if s=s′s=s^{\prime} it never splits it. Averaging over pairs,

𝔼[J(Tw)]=𝔼[|w(S1)−w(S0)|(𝟏{S0<S1}−𝟏{S1<S0})],\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[|w(S_{1})-w(S_{0})|\bigl(\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}<S_{1}\}-\mathbf{1}\{S_{1}<S_{0}\}\bigr)\bigr],

the numerator of Lemma 4 with W⁡(s,s′)=|w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)|W(s,s^{\prime})=|w(s)-w(s^{\prime})|. So averaging JJ over TwT_{w} weights each pair by how much of TwT_{w} lies between its two scores. Theorem 4 shows this is the only pair weight that arises this way.

Theorem 4 (Characterization).

Let WW be a pair weight, w:ℝ→[0,1]w:\mathbb{R}\to[0,1] nondecreasing and c>0c>0, all fixed in advance. Then

𝔼[W(S0,S1)(𝟏{S0<S1}−𝟏{S1<S0})]=c𝔼[J(Tw)]\mathbb{E}\bigl[W(S_{0},S_{1})\bigl(\mathbf{1}\{S_{0}<S_{1}\}-\mathbf{1}\{S_{1}<S_{0}\}\bigr)\bigr]=c\,\mathbb{E}[J(T_{w})]

for all distributions F0,F1F_{0},F_{1} covered by Lemma 2 (all of them if ww is smooth, all discrete ones otherwise) if and only if W⁡(s,s′)=c​|w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)|W(s,s^{\prime})=c\,|w(s)-w(s^{\prime})| for all s≠s′s\neq s^{\prime}.

The proof is in Appendix A. By Lemma 4 the left side is the numerator of AUCW\mathrm{AUC}_{W}, so a pair-weighted AUC is an average of the Youden curve exactly when it is AUCw\mathrm{AUC}_{w}. The weights must not depend on F0F_{0} and F1F_{1}. Plain AUC (W≡1W\equiv 1) fails this test: it is an average of JJ in Theorem 1 only because its weight there, FmidF^{\mathrm{mid}}, is built from the score distribution itself.

5 Coherence across models and groups

Hand (2009) objects that AUC measures different models with different rulers. Theorem 1 shows why. A lender’s costs set a risk threshold: approve everyone whose chance of repaying is above some level uu. By Theorem 1, AUC weights cutoffs by where the observations are, so on the risk scale it weights each threshold uu by how many observations have true probability near uu. That distribution differs between models: a threshold of 90% may approve the top 60% of applicants under one model and the top 40% under another. So the weight AUC puts on a given cost differs between models. By Corollary 1, the Brier skill score of the ideal forecast does not have this problem, since it weights every risk threshold equally under every model. Flach et al. (2011) reply that AUC is linear in expected loss when the cutoff is set at the score of a randomly chosen observation, rather than at the best cutoff for the costs, and the costs are drawn uniformly. Neither rule depends on the model, so as a ranking measure AUC weights every model the same way. Read as an average over cost thresholds, it does not as each model puts its own weights on the thresholds, so comparing two AUCs compares averages taken with different weights. Hand’s H-measure fixes the weights on costs in advance instead.

With nn distinct scores, write JkJ_{k} for the Youden index of acting on the top kk observations. Then Theorem 1 becomes

AUC=12+1n​(J1+⋯+Jn−1),\mathrm{AUC}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{n}\,(J_{1}+\dots+J_{n-1}), (1)

the average JJ over acting on 1,2,…,n−11,2,\dots,n-1 of the nn observations (derivation in Appendix A).

Example.

A lender scores ten applicants, five who repay (Y=1Y=1) and five who default (Y=0Y=0), with two models. From the highest score to the lowest, the labels are

Model A: 1 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 0 0,Model B: 1 1 1 0 0 0 1 0 1 0.\text{Model A: }1\,0\,1\,1\,1\,0\,1\,0\,0\,0,\qquad\text{Model B: }1\,1\,1\,0\,0\,0\,1\,0\,1\,0.

Approving the top kk gives Jk=(repayers approved)/5−(defaulters approved)/5J_{k}=(\text{repayers approved})/5-(\text{defaulters approved})/5:

kk 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
Model A .2 0 .2 .4 .6 .4 .6 .4 .2
Model B .2 .4 .6 .4 .2 0 .2 0 .2

By the share formula (1) with n=10n=10, AUC=12+3.0/10=0.80\mathrm{AUC}=\tfrac{1}{2}+3.0/10=0.80 for A and 12+2.2/10=0.72\tfrac{1}{2}+2.2/10=0.72 for B.

  1. 1.

    AUC can prefer the wrong model. Suppose a lender has funds for three loans, so it approves the three applicants with the highest scores. Only J3J_{3} matters: 0.20.2 for A and 0.60.6 for B. AUC prefers A because A ranks well near the bottom of the list, where the lender makes no decisions.

  2. 2.

    Hand’s point. Under A, no lender would approve exactly three, since approving four adds a repayer and no defaulter. Under B, approving three is what a lender with equal costs would do, since J3J_{3} is B’s largest value. Yet AUC gives J3J_{3} the same weight 1/101/10 under both models. So the lenders that AUC averages over differ between the models.

  3. 3.

    AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}. Take π=1\pi=1 on the top three and 00 elsewhere. Only pairs the policy splits, one approved and one not, count. A split pair is ordered correctly when the repayer is the one approved.

    • •

      Model A approves 22 repayers and 11 defaulter, and leaves 33 repayers and 44 defaulters. It splits 1111 of the 2525 pairs of a repayer and a defaulter: 2×4=82\times 4=8 correctly and 1×3=31\times 3=3 wrongly. So AUCπ=8/11≈0.73\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}=8/11\approx 0.73.

    • •

      Model B approves 33 repayers and no defaulters, and leaves 22 repayers and 55 defaulters. It splits 3×5=153\times 5=15 pairs, all correctly. So AUCπ=15/15=1\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}=15/15=1.

The policy Youden index Jπ=𝔼⁡[J⁡(Tπ)]J_{\pi}=\mathbb{E}[J(T_{\pi})], the numerator of AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, is J3J_{3} in the example. It compares the models under one fixed policy, so it is coherent. The denominator, the share of pairs the policy splits (11/2511/25 for A, 15/2515/25 for B), depends on the model, so the ratio is not.

The Brier skill score of the ideal forecast is also coherent, but its weights are not the decision maker’s. It counts every risk threshold equally, so a lender who approves only above a 90% chance of repaying is scored mostly on thresholds it never uses, and the Brier score also charges for miscalibration, which does not affect decisions based on the ranking. JπJ_{\pi} puts the weight on the lender’s own decisions and needs no forecast probability. The two agree, up to scale, when the lender’s probability of acting is linear in the true probability (Proposition 1).

In the example the ratio still orders the models correctly. Both models approve three applicants, so a model can do better only by approving a repayer in place of a defaulter. That adds correct splits and removes wrong ones, so AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} and JπJ_{\pi} rise together.

When the policy approves different numbers under different models, the ratio can reverse the order. Suppose the lender approves everyone whose chance of repaying is above 70%. Each model gives the applicants different chances of repaying, so the number above 70% can differ. Take the same ten applicants and two other models, C and D.

  • •

    Model C approves 11 repayer and no defaulters, and leaves 44 repayers and 55 defaulters. So Jπ=1/5−0/5=0.2J_{\pi}=1/5-0/5=0.2. It splits 1×5=51\times 5=5 pairs, all correctly, so AUCπ=5/5=1\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}=5/5=1.

  • •

    Model D approves 33 repayers and 11 defaulter, and leaves 22 repayers and 44 defaulters. So Jπ=3/5−1/5=0.4J_{\pi}=3/5-1/5=0.4. It splits 1414 pairs: 3×4=123\times 4=12 correctly and 1×2=21\times 2=2 wrongly. So AUCπ=12/14≈0.86\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}=12/14\approx 0.86.

JπJ_{\pi} prefers D, which approves two more repayers at the cost of one more defaulter. AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} prefers C only because C approves one applicant and so is judged on 55 pairs, while D is judged on 1414. To compare models, use JπJ_{\pi}; AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} rescales it into a share of pairs.

The same problem arises when one model’s AUC is compared across groups, such as two demographic groups in pretrial risk assessment. Write JgJ_{g} and FgmidF^{\mathrm{mid}}_{g} for the Youden curve and the score distribution within group gg, and Sy​gS_{yg} for the score of a class-yy observation in group gg. Within each group, Theorem 1 gives AUCg=12+𝔼⁡[Jg​(TFgmid)]\mathrm{AUC}_{g}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\mathbb{E}[J_{g}(T_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}_{g}})]. The groups have different score distributions, so their AUCs weight different cutoffs. A single policy, such as detaining everyone with a score above 7, is one cutoff for both groups, and it falls at a different share of each group. Here the scores are on a common scale, so the fix is simple: choose one weight ww for both groups and compare

𝔼⁡[Jg​(Tw)]=𝔼⁡[w⁡(S1​g)]−𝔼⁡[w⁡(S0​g)],\mathbb{E}[J_{g}(T_{w})]=\mathbb{E}[w(S_{1g})]-\mathbb{E}[w(S_{0g})],

which by Lemma 3 needs only the mean of ww in each class of each group. The natural choice is the policy itself, w=πw=\pi, which compares the groups at the decisions actually made. Another possible choice is the score distribution of the two groups combined, which keeps AUC’s weighting by where the scores are but makes it the same for both groups. This weight depends on the mix of the groups, and whether it is a sensible default remains to be checked.

6 Conclusion

AUC, the Brier score and AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} are built on averages of the same curve, the Youden index J⁡(t)J(t), and differ in how they weight the cutoffs. AUC weights them by where the scores are, the Brier score by the true probability, and AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} by the decision maker’s probability of acting. So when AUC and the Brier score rank two models differently, part of the disagreement is about which decisions count.

This matters most when comparing models. AUC’s weights come from each model’s own scores, so two models’ AUCs count different decisions. The Brier score weights every model the same way, but its weights are not the decision maker’s, and it also charges for calibration. When the decision policy π\pi is known, models should be compared by the policy Youden index JπJ_{\pi}, the expected share of class 1 the policy acts on minus the expected share of class 0. It needs only the mean of π\pi in each class. AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} puts this on the scale of a share of pairs, but its denominator depends on the model, so it should not be used alone to rank models. When the policy is unknown, JπJ_{\pi} can be reported for a range of plausible policies.

Selecting a model is this comparison on held-out data. Cross-validation keeps the candidate with the best score, so the score decides which decisions count. If the score is AUC, the selected model can be one that ranks well where the decision maker never acts. If it is AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi}, the denominator depends on the model, so it can reverse the order JπJ_{\pi} gives (Section 5). When the policy is known, the score to maximize is JπJ_{\pi}. Hand’s H-measure fixes a distribution of costs and scores each model at its own best cutoff. JπJ_{\pi} is the criterion when the policy is already fixed and that cutoff will not be retuned.

Several questions remain. JJ weights the two classes equally, which in cost terms means a cost ratio that depends on the base rate (Smits, 2010). Extending the results to TPR−k​FPR\mathrm{TPR}-k\,\mathrm{FPR} is ongoing work. We do not know whether another normalization of AUCπ\mathrm{AUC}_{\pi} keeps both coherence and the reading as a share of pairs. Inference when π\pi is itself estimated remains to be worked out. The results also assume a binary outcome.

Appendix A Proofs

Proof of Lemma 1.

By Bayes’ rule,

F1​(t)=P⁡(S≤t∣Y=1)=F⁡(t)​P⁡(Y=1∣S≤t)P⁡(Y=1).F_{1}(t)=P(S\leq t\mid Y=1)=F(t)\,\frac{P(Y=1\mid S\leq t)}{P(Y=1)}.

Since rr is nondecreasing, P⁡(Y=1∣S≤t)≤P⁡(Y=1∣S>t)P(Y=1\mid S\leq t)\leq P(Y=1\mid S>t), and P⁡(Y=1)P(Y=1) is an average of the two, so P⁡(Y=1∣S≤t)≤P⁡(Y=1)P(Y=1\mid S\leq t)\leq P(Y=1) and F1​(t)≤F​(t)F_{1}(t)\leq F(t). The same argument for class 0 gives F0​(t)≥F⁡(t)F_{0}(t)\geq F(t). ∎

Proof of Lemma 2.

(a) Integrating by parts,

The identity says these are equal, so W⁡(s,s′)=c⁡(w⁡(s′)−w⁡(s))=c​|w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)|W(s,s^{\prime})=c\bigl(w(s^{\prime})-w(s)\bigr)=c\,|w(s)-w(s^{\prime})|, using that ww is nondecreasing. Each pair s<s′s<s^{\prime} gets its own choice of distributions, so this holds for all s<s′s<s^{\prime}. For s>s′s>s^{\prime}, WW is symmetric, so W⁡(s,s′)=W⁡(s′,s)=c|w⁡(s′)−w⁡(s)|=c​|w⁡(s)−w⁡(s′)|W(s,s^{\prime})=W(s^{\prime},s)=c\,|w(s^{\prime})-w(s)|=c\,|w(s)-w(s^{\prime})|. ∎

Derivation of (1).

Let the scores s1<⋯<sns_{1}<\dots<s_{n} each have probability 1/n1/n. Then P⁡(S<sk)=(k−1)/nP(S<s_{k})=(k-1)/n and P⁡(S=sk)=1/nP(S=s_{k})=1/n, so

Fmid​(sk)=k−1n+12​n=k−12n,Fmid​(sk)−Fmid​(sk−1)=1n.F^{\mathrm{mid}}(s_{k})=\frac{k-1}{n}+\frac{1}{2n}=\frac{k-\tfrac{1}{2}}{n},\qquad F^{\mathrm{mid}}(s_{k})-F^{\mathrm{mid}}(s_{k-1})=\frac{1}{n}.

By Lemma 3 and Lemma 2(b),

𝔼⁡[J⁡(TFmid)]=∑k=2n1n​J​(sk−1).\mathbb{E}[J(T_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}})]=\sum_{k=2}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\,J(s_{k-1}).

The cutoff sk−1s_{k-1} acts on the scores above sk−1s_{k-1}, which are the top n−k+1n-k+1, so J⁡(sk−1)=Jn−k+1J(s_{k-1})=J_{n-k+1}. As kk runs from 22 to nn, n−k+1n-k+1 runs from n−1n-1 down to 11, so

𝔼⁡[J⁡(TFmid)]=1n​(J1+⋯+Jn−1),\mathbb{E}[J(T_{F^{\mathrm{mid}}})]=\frac{1}{n}\,(J_{1}+\dots+J_{n-1}),

and Theorem 1 gives (1). ∎
